title: Around the world near the pole
hook: Around the world is 40,000 km. Is it always?

knows: that the equator is about 40,000 km around
that lines of longitude meet at the poles
doesNotKnow: how quickly circles of latitude shrink near the pole
that a lap at 89°N is only about 700 km

misconception: Going around the world always means about 40,000 km.
objective: The learner can say that a circle of latitude has length 2πR cos(latitude), so a lap at 89°N is about 700 km, under 2% of the equator.
keyState: The equator or 60°N lap seen first (big), then 89°N (about 700 km), with the map zoomed and the scale bar showing it.

claims.text: Once around the world along 89°N is about 700 km.
claims.source: 2πR cos 89° with R = 6,371.0088 km = 698.6 km (builder node run; Demo.tsx lapKm). Matches the cm-geography brief. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 698.6 km.

claims.text: Once around the equator is about 40,030 km on the lesson's sphere, and 89°N is under 2% of that.
claims.source: 2πR = 40,030.2 km; 698.6 / 40,030 = 1.75%. The real equator is 40,075 km on WGS84 (from memory); the question says 'about 40,000'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 40,030 km; ratio 1.75%.

claims.text: At 85°N one lap is about 3,490 km.
claims.source: 2πR cos 85° = 3,488.9 km (builder node run). Quoted in the reveal only if 85°N was visited. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 3,488.9 km.

claims.text: A circle of latitude has radius R × cos(latitude); cos 89° is about 0.017.
claims.source: Geometry of the sphere; cos 89° = 0.01745. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): cos 89 = 0.01745.

claims.text: One degree from the pole, the circle is about 220 km across.
claims.source: Diameter measured over the surface: 2 × (1° × π/180 × R) = 222.4 km, shown as 220 km (r10 rounding). Demo.tsx fromPoleKm. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): 2 x 111.2 = 222.4 km, shown as 220.

claims.text: 89°N lies on the drifting sea ice of the Arctic Ocean.
claims.source: The North Pole region is ocean about 4 km deep, covered by drifting sea ice (NSIDC, 'Arctic sea ice' pages; from memory). Seasonal open water is possible; the reveal says 'if you could walk it'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Hedged by 'if you could walk it'; open water in leads is possible.

claims.text: On a map centred on the pole (azimuthal equidistant), distances from the pole are true.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, azimuthal equidistant (from memory). The scale bar is computed from the same projection scale. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Azimuthal equidistant: distances along lines through the centre are true.

recall.question: Why is a walk 'around the world' along 89°N far shorter than along the equator?
options: Because the ice slows you down
Because circles of latitude shrink with the cosine of latitude, almost to nothing near the pole
It isn't: every lap around the world is about 40,000 km
recall.why: A parallel's radius is R cos(latitude); at 89°N cos is 0.017, so the lap is about 700 km instead of 40,000.
